title: Silence
summary: Silence, also tracked as Whisper Spider, is a financially motivated group that public reporting from Group-IB and others describes as active from around 2016 and based in Russian speaking regions, with attacks on banks and payment processing systems across Europe, Asia and Latin America. The tradecraft reported combines email compromise to learn internal payment routines, custom remote access and proxy tooling, and direct interaction with automated teller machines, including attempts to force cash dispensing at scheduled times. Reporting also describes the group recruiting insiders at banks to obtain knowledge and access that no external tool can provide. That insider element is the key lesson for defenders: monitoring for transactional anomalies, enforcing separation of duties, and watching for unusual cash machine activity are as important as endpoint detection, and attribution to a single organisation remains an assessment rather than a settled fact.

beginner.definition: Silence is a criminal group that steals money from banks. Public reports say it started around 2016 and works from Russian speaking regions. It attacked banks in Europe, Asia and South America. Another name for the same activity is Whisper Spider. Reports also describe the group paying people inside banks for help, which is called using an insider.
beginner.whyItMatters: Technical controls cannot stop an employee who shares procedures on purpose. So banks must watch transactions for unusual patterns, not only networks for unusual files. Cash machine activity is a clear signal, because real withdrawals follow customer behaviour. Separating duties also helps, so no single person controls a whole payment process. Insider risk is a security problem, not only a human resources problem.
howItWorks: The attackers gather details about staff through email tricks and from public information.
They steal mail access so that they can read internal payment and procedure documents.
They quietly install remote access tools on the computers inside the bank network.
They pay or persuade an employee to get details about the cash machine systems.
They then attempt to make cash machines dispense money at the times they choose.
They then move the money through bank accounts held by their helpers and couriers.
beginner.example: Picture a vault with a very good door and a very careful guard. The thieves do not attack the door. They befriend the guard, learn the schedule, and walk in when the vault is open for a routine delivery. The strongest lock in the building cannot help if someone inside holds it open for them.
takeaways: Inside help can defeat strong technical controls, so watch for unusual process changes.
Review cash machine and transfer activity against normal customer behaviour.
Split duties so that no single person can complete a large payment alone.

objectives: Explain how insider involvement changes the defensive problem for a bank.
Describe how transaction monitoring detects fraud that endpoint tools miss.
Explain the principle of separation of duties in payment processes.
Outline how stolen internal documents support a payment attack.
Explain why group attribution should be stated with confidence levels.
